question.text: A Cat III AIF creates a SIDE-POCKET when:

answer.text: It wants to reduce management-fee expense

A specific asset becomes illiquid, stressed, or materially hard-to-value, and the manager segregates it so that NAV of the rest of the fund remains tradeable and fair to subscribing/redeeming investors
The fund wants to bypass the 2x leverage cap
The manager wishes to concentrate all profitable trades

explanation.text: The Logic: Side-pocketing isolates a troubled asset (illiquid, stressed, hard-to-value) so NAV of the main scheme is not distorted by mark-to-model uncertainty on that one asset. Without side-pocketing, new subscribers would inherit the stress (unfair) and exiting investors would exit at arbitrary marks (also unfair). SEBI permits side-pocketing in Cat III with proper disclosure. The Trap: Options A, C, D are fabricated motivations. Side-pocketing is a fairness tool, not a fee/leverage gimmick. Cross-Exam Context: XIX-D briefly covers side-pocketing (rare in Cat I/II). XIX-C / XIX-E test Cat III mechanics. Manager's Pro-Tip: Establish your side-pocket triggers and valuation policy in the PPM BEFORE you need one — trying to side-pocket during a crisis without a pre-documented policy invites investor litigation.
